concepts.title: Universal Law of Gravitation
concepts.body: The universal law of gravitation states that every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This force acts along the line joining the centers of the two objects. For example, the Earth pulls you towards its center, keeping you grounded.

concepts.title: Free Fall and Acceleration Due to Gravity (g)
concepts.body: Free fall is the motion of an object under the influence of gravity alone, without any other forces acting on it. All objects in free fall near the Earth's surface accelerate at the same rate, approximately 9.8 m/s^2, regardless of their mass. For instance, a feather and a hammer dropped in a vacuum will hit the ground simultaneously.

concepts.title: Mass vs Weight
concepts.body: Mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object and remains constant regardless of location. Weight, on the other hand, is the force exerted on an object due to gravity and varies depending on the gravitational field strength. For example, your mass is the same on Earth and the Moon, but your weight is less on the Moon because of its weaker gravity.

formulas.title: Universal Gravitational Force
formulas.body: F = G x m1 x m2 / r^2 (F in newton N, m in kg, r in m). Here, F is the gravitational force, G is the gravitational constant (6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2), m1 and m2 are the masses of the two objects, and r is the distance between their centers. This formula is used to calculate the gravitational force between two objects.

formulas.title: Weight
formulas.body: W = m x g (W in newton N, m in kg, g in m/s^2). Here, W is the weight of the object, m is its mass, and g is the acceleration due to gravity. This formula is used to determine the weight of an object based on its mass and the gravitational field strength.

examples.title: Everyday Example
examples.body: When you jump, you are momentarily in free fall, accelerating downward at 9.8 m/s^2 due to Earth's gravity. This is why you come back down after jumping.

examples.title: Applied Example
examples.body: Satellites orbiting the Earth are in a continuous state of free fall. The gravitational force between the Earth and the satellite provides the centripetal force needed to keep the satellite in orbit.

mcqs.question: What is the acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface?
mcqs.explanation: The acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 m/s^2. This is a fundamental constant in physics and is the same for all objects in free fall near the Earth's surface.

mcqs.question: If the mass of an object is 10 kg, what is its weight on Earth? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
mcqs.explanation: Weight is calculated using the formula W = m x g. For a mass of 10 kg and g = 9.8 m/s^2, the weight is 10 x 9.8 = 98 N. The other options are incorrect because they either ignore the value of g or miscalculate the product.

mcqs.question: Two objects of masses 5 kg and 10 kg are placed 2 meters apart. What is the gravitational force between them? (G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2)
mcqs.explanation: The gravitational force is calculated using F = G x m1 x m2 / r^2. Substituting the given values, F = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 5 x 10 / (2)^2 = 8.34 x 10^-10 N. The other options are incorrect because they either miscalculate the product or the division by r^2.
